notes.urn:cts:latinLit:phi0474.phi072.perseus-: 1.1: 'in Academicis' may refer to Cicero's Academica. 2.1: a lacuna follows in the text; the preface breaks off and the translation of Plato begins abruptly at 3.1. 14.1: 'requisitum' is obelised as corrupt in the edition; the sense required (cf. Plato 32a) is 'depth' or 'thickness', i.e. 'nothing in it were [of depth]'. 15.1: 'anima' here renders Greek aēr and is translated 'air'.

Text is lacunose at 28/29 (marked * * *): the account of what happens when reason turns on intelligible things breaks off, and the start of 29 is fragmentary ('...ius natura converteret'), so the opening clause is rendered as far as it can be read. In 23 the definitions of the harmonic and arithmetic means are compressed; bracketed words supply the sense. 'Lucifer' is the planet Venus.

36.1: the text is corrupt (marked † in the edition: 'de quo et idem ... celaret'); 'celaret' is probably for 'ciet/ageret' or similar, and the sense 'revolve in the same and one way' is conjectural. 37.1: the clause on conjunctions ('eorum qui prope copulentur...') is syntactically awkward in the Latin; rendered loosely. 38.1: Cicero's own equation of daimones with Lares is tentative ('opinor').

The edition marks lacunae (* * *) at the end of 48.1 and 52.1; Cicero's text breaks off mid-sentence at both points, and a substantial passage (on sight and mirrors, Plato 43e-46a) is missing between 48.1 and 49.1, so 49.1 begins abruptly. In 48.1 'illi' is taken as the circuits (ambitus) of the soul. In 49.1 'altitudinem adsumpsit' is taken as the mirror's surface being curved upward at the sides (Plato's concave mirror).

nodes.text: Many things have been written by me, both in the Academics, against the natural philosophers, and [many] often debated with Publius Nigidius in the manner and method of Carneades. For that man was not only furnished with all the other arts that are worthy of a free man, but was also a keen and diligent investigator of those things which seem to be wrapped up by nature; in short, this is my judgement: after those noble Pythagoreans, whose school was in a certain way extinguished after it had flourished for several centuries in Italy and Sicily, he arose to renew it.

When he, returning to Rome from an embassy, had waited for me at Ephesus as I was setting out for Cilicia, and Cratippus had come to the same place from Mytilene to greet and visit me, Cratippus, in my judgement easily the foremost of all the Peripatetics whom I at least have heard, I was very glad both to see Nigidius and to get to know Cratippus. And the first part of the time, that of greeting, we spent in questioning * * *

What is it that always is and has no coming-into-being, and what is it that comes into being and never is? Of these the one is grasped by understanding and reason, being always one and the same; the other, which sense devoid of reason brings to opinion, being wholly a matter of opinion, comes into being and perishes, and can never truly be. Moreover, everything that comes into being must come into being from some cause; for when the cause is removed, the origin of nothing can be found.

Therefore if he who sets out to accomplish some work looks to that form which is always the same and sets this before himself as a model, he must necessarily produce a splendid work; but if he looks to that which comes into being, he will never attain the beauty he seeks. The whole heaven, then, or world, or whatever other name it delights in, let it be so named by us—

concerning which let us first consider what must be considered at the outset in every inquiry: whether it has always been, generated by no coming-into-being, or whether it arose from some beginning in time. It arose, since it is seen and touched and is bodily in every part. And all such things move the senses, and the things that move the senses settle into opinion; and these, we said, have a coming-into-being and are generated, and nothing can be generated without causes.

Now, to find him who is as it were the parent of this universe is difficult, and, once you have found him, to declare him to the multitude is forbidden. So we must consider again which model the maker of so great a work imitated: that which is always one and the same and like itself, or that which we call generated and having come into being. Yet if this world is beautiful and if its craftsman is good, he surely preferred to imitate the form of eternity; but if otherwise, which it is not right even to say, he followed a generated model instead of the eternal one.

There is no doubt, then, that he preferred to follow eternity, since there is nothing more beautiful than the world and nothing more excellent than its builder. So, though generated, it has been made after that which is grasped by reason and wisdom and is contained in unchangeable eternity. From this it follows that this world which we see must necessarily be an everlasting likeness of something eternal. But in every inquiry the beginning of the reasoning is the most difficult part. Concerning the things we have said, then, let this be the first distinction.

Every discourse seems to have a kinship with the things it sets out. So when discourse treats of what is stable and unchangeable, let it be such as cannot be refuted or overthrown. But when it has entered upon things imitated and fashioned as likenesses, it thinks it does well if it attains likelihood of the truth. For as eternity stands to what has come into being, so truth stands to belief. Therefore if, in discoursing on the nature of the gods and the origin of the world, we perhaps fall short of what we long for in mind, namely that the whole discourse, clearly and plainly set out, should be consistent with itself and agree with itself in every part, it will certainly be no wonder, and you ought to be content if probable things are said. For it is fair to remember both that I who speak am a man and that you who judge are men, so that, if probable things are said, you should seek nothing further.

Let us seek, then, the cause that drove him who contrived these things to seek an origin of things and a new construction. He excelled, clearly, in goodness; and the good man envies no one; therefore he generated all things like himself. This, surely, is the most just cause of generating the world. For since god had resolved to fill the world with all good things and to mix in nothing bad, so far as nature permitted, he took to himself whatever there was that fell under the sense of sight, not calm and at rest but moving without measure and fluctuating, and brought it from disorder into order; for he judged this to be better.

For it neither is nor ever was right for him who was best to make anything except what is most beautiful. Having therefore taken thought, he found that of the things visible by nature nothing unintelligent was, taken as a whole kind, more excellent than the intelligent. Therefore he enclosed intelligence in soul, and soul in body. Thus he reckoned that the work was made most beautiful. For this reason we should not hesitate to declare, if only anything can be investigated by conjecture, that this world is a living being, and that it is intelligent and established by divine providence.

This being laid down, we must consider what follows: in the likeness of which of the living beings god followed in fashioning the world. Certainly of none of the living beings known to us; for they are all divided into certain kinds, or begun and in no part complete; and nothing like the imperfect and incomplete can be beautiful. Let us say, then, that the world is like that of which every living being is as it were a certain small part, whether seen singly or in its whole kind. All the living beings, then, that are discerned by the mind and understood by reason are comprehended in the embrace of reason and intelligence, just as men and beasts and all things that fall under sight are comprehended by this world.

For since god wished to make the world like that which can be understood as most beautiful in the nature of things, and which is in every part most complete, he made a single visible living being in which all living beings would be contained. Have we rightly, then, called the world one, or would it have been better and truer to say there were several or countless? One, surely, since it was made after the model. For that which embraces all the living beings that are understood by reason cannot exist along with another. For then there would have to be yet another living being to contain it, of which they would be parts, being superior living beings, and this heaven would be a likeness of that ultimate one, not of the nearer one. So that none of this should happen, and so that this world should be most like the complete living being in this very respect, that it was alone and one, god therefore created this world single and only-begotten.

Now everything that has come into being must be bodily and visible and also tangible. Further, nothing devoid of fire can be seen and perceived, nor indeed can anything be touched that lacks solidity, and nothing is solid that has no share of earth; therefore god, setting out to make the world, first joined earth and fire. But any two things require some third thing to cohere, and want as it were a knot and bond. And the most fitting and most beautiful of bonds is that which makes, of itself and of the things it binds, as much of a unity as possible. This is best achieved by what in Greek is called *analogia*, and in Latin (for I must be bold, since these terms are being newly coined by me for the first time) can be called *comparatio* or *proportio* [proportion].

For whenever, of three numbers or figures or things of any kinds whatever, it happens that the middle term is related to the last as the first is to it, and conversely, as the last is to the middle, so the middle is to the first, then the middle becomes both first and last, and the last and first become middle; so necessity compels that the things which had been separate become the same; and when they have become the same, the result is that all are one. Now if the body of the universe were spread out flat and even, and nothing in it were † required, a single interposed mean would bind together both itself and the things between which it was placed.

But since solidity was sought for the world, and solids are never coupled by one mean but always by two, it came about that god placed water and air between fire and earth and related them to one another and joined them in proportion, so that as fire is to air, so air is to water, and what air is to water, water is in proportion to earth. By this conjunction the heaven was so fitted together that it falls under sight and touch. And so, both for this reason and from these things, four in number, the body of the world was made, bound by the proportion I have described; from which it embraces itself in a certain harmonious friendship and affection and coheres so fittingly that it can in no way be dissolved except by him by whom it was bound together.

Now all the parts of those four things which I mentioned above were so placed in the whole world that no part of this kind went outside it, and that in this universe all those kinds were present in their entirety, and this for these reasons: first, that the world, a living being, might be complete from complete parts; next, that it might be one, with no part left from which another might be begotten; lastly, that no disease or old age could touch it.

For every compound of body is weakened and broken by the force of heat or cold or by some violent impact, and is driven to disease and old age. This, then, was the reasoning held by god, the maker and builder of the world: that he should complete one work, whole and complete, out of all things whole and complete, which would be free of all disease and senility. And he gave it a shape both most akin to it and most seemly. For the living being by which he wished all the remaining living beings to be contained, he shaped with that shape by which alone all the remaining shapes are enclosed, and he fashioned it globular, which the Greeks call *sphaireides*, every point of whose extremity is reached by equal radii from the middle; and he so turned it, as on a lathe, that he could make nothing rounder, so that it should have no roughness, no unevenness, nothing cut by angles, nothing by windings, nothing projecting, nothing hollowed, and all its parts most like all [the others], because in his judgement likeness was better than unlikeness.

And he surrounded the whole figure of the world with complete smoothness. For it needed no eyes, because nothing had been left outside that could be seen, nor ears, because nothing even that could be heard; nor was the outer edge of the world surrounded by air, so that it should require breathing; nor indeed did it want either nourishment for its body or the removal of food digested and used up; for no loss could occur, nor any addition, nor indeed was there anywhere from which [it could]. And so it nourished itself by its own consumption and decay, since it itself, through itself and from itself, both suffered and did all things. For he who joined and founded these things thought that the world should be content with itself and not need another.

And so he attached no hands to it, since there was nothing either to be taken or to be repelled, nor feet or other limbs with which to support the body's walking. For he gave the heaven that motion which was most suited to its shape, which alone of the seven motions most stirs mind and intelligence. And so it is twisted and turned about itself in one and the same revolution. The six remaining motions he separated from it, and so freed it from all wandering. For this revolution, then, which needed no feet or step, he did not give it limbs for walking.

Considering these things concerning the god who was at some time to be, the god who was made it smooth and on every side even, equal from the middle to the extremity, and complete and perfect out of perfect and complete [parts]. And as he placed the soul in its middle, so he stretched it through the whole; then he surrounded it with body and clothed it from outside, and enclosed it in a heaven that wanders alone, revolving and driven in a circle, which because of its excellence could easily be at one with itself and would not want another, being sufficiently known and familiar to itself.

Thus that eternal god begot this perfectly blessed god. But he did not begin the soul, as we spoke just now, only then, when he had made the body for it; for it would not be right for the greater to obey the lesser; but we say many things inconsiderately and at random. God, however, begot the soul prior both in origin and in excellence, and set it as master and ruler over the obedient body, and he constructed it in some such way as this: from that substance which is indivisible and always of one mode and like itself, and from that which comes to be divisible in bodies, he mixed from the two, in the middle, a third kind of substance, which should be of the nature of the same and of that of the other, and he placed it between the indivisible and that which was divisible in body.

Having taken these three, he blended them into one form, and he joined that nature which we have called [the nature] of the other, which shuns and is averse to that coupling, by force with the same; and mixing these with the substance, when he had made one out of three, he divided this very thing into such portions as was fitting. Each portion he now blended of the same and of the other and of the substance. And that division was as follows: at the start he took one portion from the whole, then a second, double the first portion, then a third, which was one and a half times the second and three times the first, then a fourth, which was double the second, next a fifth, three times the third, then a sixth, eight times the first, lastly a seventh, which exceeded the first twenty-seven times.

Then he set about filling the double and triple intervals, again cutting portions from the whole; these he placed in the intervals so that in each there were two means (for I hardly dare to say 'medieties', which the Greeks call *mesotetes*; but let it be understood as if I had said so; for it will be clearer), one of them exceeding [one] extreme and exceeded by [the other] by the same fraction [of the extremes], the other exceeding [one] extreme and exceeded [by the other] by an equal number. And when intervals of three to two and four to three and nine to eight had arisen from these links in the first intervals, he filled all the four-to-three intervals with the nine-to-eight interval, leaving a small portion of each.

And when the interval of this small portion was left, number had to number in the extremes the same proportion and ratio as two hundred and fifty-six has to two hundred and forty-three; and thus he had now used up all that mixture from which he cut these [portions]. This whole combination, then, he split lengthwise into two, and fitting middle to middle he crossed them as in the form of an X, then bent them into a circle, so that they were joined both each with itself and with each other at the junction opposite [the crossing], and he embraced them on every side with that motion whose circuit was always in the same [place] and was moved in the same way.

And so, when he had embraced one as the outer circle, the other as the inner, he marked the former as [the circle] of the nature of the same, the latter of the other; and the one which was of the same he turned along the side to the right, and the other, the nearer, he directed along the diagonal to the left; but he gave supremacy to the upper one, which alone he left undivided. The inner one, however, when he had divided it into six parts, he ordered to move as seven unequal circles, at double and triple intervals, with courses contrary to one another. Of these he made three equal in speed, but four unequal both among themselves and to the remaining three.

Then, when that god, the creator of the world, had begotten the soul from his own mind and will, only then did he lay beneath the soul everything that was compacted and bodily, and set it within, and so, fitting middle to middle, coupled them. Thus the soul, setting out from the middle, threw itself round the extremity of the heaven from the uppermost region in a circular compass, and turning itself, it initiated the divine beginning of everlasting and wise life.

And the body of the heaven was made visible, but the soul escapes the gaze of the eyes. It is, however, the one among all things that has command of and a share in reason and concord, which in Greek is *harmonia*, [concord] of everlasting things that fall under the intelligence, and nothing better than it has been produced by the best and most excellent begetter; for it is joined from the same and from the nature of the other with substance added, compacted in proportion by a blending of three parts, and turning upon itself, when it lays hold of changeable substance and again when it lays hold of indivisible and simple [substance], it is moved through all of itself and discerns what is of the kind of the same and what of the other, and judges the rest: what is most fitting for each thing, what befalls in each place or manner or time, and what distinction there is between the things that come to be and those that are always the same.

Now true reason, which is concerned with the things that are always the same and with those that change, when it is moved in the same and in the other by itself, without voice and without any sound, when it touches that part where sense can be stirred, and the circle of that kind, the other, unchanged and straight, announces everything to the soul and mind, then firm and true opinions and assents are produced; but when it turns among those things which, remaining always the same, are grasped not by sense but by intelligence * * * So by divine reason and mind, for the origin of time, the course of the sun and moon was devised

* * * nature should turn, so that the course of the moon should go round the earth nearest, and the circuit of the sun should be next to it above the earth. Then Lucifer and the holy star of Mercury have a course equal in speed to the sun, but a certain contrary force, and in that concourse which Lucifer, Mercury and the sun have among themselves, they overtake one another and are overtaken in turn.

As for the remaining stars, what reason there was for placing them and what their placement is must be deferred to another discussion, lest a longer account be given of what had to be touched on than of that for the sake of which we touch on it. When, therefore, each of those stars by which the measure of time was to be marked had gained its fitting course, and living beings had arisen, their bodies bound by living bonds, and had learned to obey command, then, running from the slanting motion of the nature of the other into the motion of the nature of the same, and clinging to it and held back, some traversing a greater circle and others a lesser, more slowly those [on] the greater, more swiftly those [on] the lesser, by the motion of the one and same nature those which moved most swiftly seemed to be overtaken by the slower, and, when they were overtaking, to be overtaken.

For every circle of theirs turned as if with the twist of a spiral, because, advancing in two directions at once contrary to each other, they brought it about that what was slowest came nearest to the swiftest. And so that there might be some clear measure to show the swiftnesses and slownesses in the eight courses, the god himself kindled the sun like a light at the second circuit above the earth, so that the heaven might shine as brightly as possible for all, and so that living beings to whom it was right to be taught might learn the nature and force of numbers from the motion of the same and of that which is similar.

Night, then, and day, produced in this way and for these reasons, make up one circuit of the circle, the wisest and best; a month, when the moon, having traversed its course, has overtaken the sun; a year, when the sun has completed and travelled through its whole circle.

But the circuits of the other stars men do not know, apart from very few, and they neither call them by name nor measure them against one another by number. And so they do not know that these wanderings of the stars, endowed with infinite multitude and wonderful variety, are the very thing which is rightly called time. And yet this can be seen and understood: that, with the complete and perfect number of time, the complete and perfect year is fulfilled only when the eight circuits, their courses completed, have returned to the same starting point, and when the circle that is the same and always like itself has measured them out.

For these reasons, then, the stars were born, which, passing through the heaven, should turn back at the summer and winter solstices, so that this whole living being which we see might be as like as possible to that living being which we perceive with the mind, in imitation of its eternity.

And the rest, up to the birth of time, he had fashioned stamped from those things which he was imitating; but because he had not yet enclosed every living being within the world, in that respect the likeness of the image fell short of the model set before it. So, as many and such forms of living beings as mind, looking upon the form of things, could discern, so many and such he resolved to fashion in this world.

Now there were four kinds of living beings: one divine and heavenly, the second winged and of the air, the third of the water, the fourth of the land. The form of the divine animation he made mostly of fire, so that it might be most brilliant and most beautiful to look on. And since he wished to make it like the nature of the universe, he rounded it for revolving, and made it the companion of the wisdom of the best mind, and distributed it evenly around the whole heaven, so that the Greeks rightly name this, adorned with variety, *kosmos* and we a shining world.

And to the divine beings he gave two kinds of motion: one, that it should be always in the same [place] † and should [revolve] in the same and one way for all; the other, that it should be driven forward by the revolution of the same and similar. But of the five remaining motions he wished it to be bereft and free, unmoving and standing. Of this kind are those stars which, fixed in the heaven, do not move from their place; they are living beings, and divine, and for that reason they cling to their seats and remain forever. But those which glide with a wandering and changeable straying were produced as we said above.

Next, the earth, our nurse, which is held up on an axis passing through it, the maker of day and night and likewise their guardian, he wished to be the oldest of all the gods who were born within the heaven. But the dances of the gods and their concourses with one another, and what revolutions and what advances occur in their circles, and, when they almost touch one another, which of them are joined closely and in contrary region, and behind which or before which they glide, and at what times they hide from our sight and, emerging again, strike terror into those without reason — if we were to try to explain these in words without any model of these things set before the eyes, the labour would be undertaken in vain. But let this be enough said by us, and let what we have set out about the nature of the gods who are seen and who have been born have this end.

As for the rest, whom the Greeks call *daimones* and our people, I think, *Lares*, if indeed this can be thought rightly translated, both to know and to declare their birth is a greater task than we would dare to profess to write. We must surely believe the ancient and early men, as they say, who said that they were the offspring of gods, and so they handed down their names to us. And they were best able to know their own begetters, and it is hard to withhold belief from those born of gods, although their account is confirmed neither by arguments nor by sure reasons; but since they seem to speak of matters known to them, we must obey ancient law and custom.

So then, as has been handed down by them, let the birth of these gods be held and spoken of thus: that we record Oceanus and Salacia as begotten and brought forth by the seed of Caelus and the conceiving of Terra; from these Saturn and Ops; next Jupiter and Juno, and the rest whom we see spoken of and called brothers and kin to one another, and their, to use an old word, *prosapia* (lineage).

When, therefore, all had been created, both those who move and show themselves openly and those who are revealed to us so far as they themselves wish, then the god who begot all things speaks to them: “Attend to this, you who have sprung from the seed of gods: of those works of which I am parent and maker, these are indissoluble against my will; although everything bound together can be loosed, yet it is by no means the part of a good [being] to wish to dissolve what is bound by reason. But since you have been born, you cannot indeed be immortal and indissoluble; yet you will in no way be dissolved, nor will any fates of death destroy you, nor any deceit stronger than my counsel, which is a greater bond for your perpetuity than those by which you were bound together at the time when you were being begotten.

Learn, then, what I intend: three kinds remain for us, and those mortal; if they are passed over, the completion of the heaven will not be perfect. For it will not hold all kinds of living beings in its embrace; yet it must hold them, so that nothing may be lacking from it. If these were made by me myself, they could equal the life of the gods. So that they may be begotten in mortal condition, then, you take this up: beget them and imitate my power, which you remember I used at your birth. Among them, those who shall be created such that they ought to be as it were kinsmen of the immortal gods, let them be called of divine kind, and let them hold the leadership of all living beings, and obey you willingly by right and law; their beginning and seed shall be handed to you by me, and you, to what will be immortal, weave on a mortal part. So living beings will arise whom you may nourish while alive and receive into your bosom when spent.”

So he spoke. Then he returned to the earlier mixing bowl; in it, blending the whole soul of universal nature, he mixed it, and pouring in the remains of the earlier mixture he made it even in almost the same way, except that [they were] not so pure as those which are always the same, but he took from them a second and even a third [grade].

So, when the whole had been composed, he distributed a number of souls equal to the stars and joined each one to each, and so set them as it were in the chariot of the universe, and showed them the laws of fate and necessity, and made clear that the first birth would be one for all, and that measured and constant and diminished by none; and that when the souls had been sown and as it were scattered, it would come about that at fixed intervals of time there would arise a living being most fitted for the worship of the gods.

But since the nature of the human race was twofold, the case stood thus: that the superior kind would be those who were to be men. And when he had implanted souls in bodies by necessity, and when there was now addition to the bodies, now departure, it was necessary first that there arise one sensation, common to all, stirred by a more violent motion and joined to nature; then love mixed with pleasure and distress; after that anger and fear and the remaining emotions of the soul, companions of the former and also at variance with them as their opposites; whoever governs these by reason will live justly, but whoever gives himself up to them, unjustly.

And he who has completed rightly and honourably the course of living given by nature will return to that star to which he was fitted; but whoever has lived immoderately and intemperately, him a second birth will transfer into a woman's shape, and if not even then he makes an end of his vices, he will be tossed about yet more heavily and transferred into the shapes of cattle and wild beasts most like his own character, and he will not see an end of his ills before he has begun to follow that revolution of the same and similar which he had innate and implanted within himself. This will come about when he has driven out by reason those turbulent and irrational things that have settled in [him] from fire, air, water and earth, and has reached the first and best condition of the soul.

When he had laid these things out thus, and had placed himself beyond all blame and cause if any harm or vice should afterwards occur, he scattered and as it were sowed some into the earth, some into the moon, some into the remaining parts of the world which are set as signs and marks of the spans of time. After that sowing he allowed the gods, so to speak, the younger ones, to fashion mortal bodies, and whatever remained of the human soul that ought to be added, all of that and what followed from it, to finish and complete; then to show themselves leaders and guides to this living being, and to rule and steer its life as finely as possible, in so far as it did not itself, though well made, seek out some misery for itself by its own fault.

And he indeed who had composed all things remained steadfastly in his own state; but those who had been created by him, when they had learned their parent's order, followed it. And so, when they had received the immortal principle of the mortal living being, imitating their begetter and maker, they borrowed from the world particles of fire and earth and water and air, to be paid back again, and joined them together, not with the same bonds by which they themselves had been bound, but with such as could not be seen because of their smallness; with close-set little wedges, as it were, fused in, they made out of all of them one body, and in it, flowing in and flowing out, they bound the circuits of the divine soul.

And so those [circuits], plunged into a river, neither held nor were held, but with great force now carried, now were carried. Thus that whole living being was indeed moved, but immoderately and at random, so that it was borne with six motions. For both forwards and backwards, and to the left and to the right, and upwards and downwards, now this way, now that * * *

But if it has settled on a bright surface, then either the same form or sometimes a changed one is given back, when the fire of the eyes has mingled and joined itself with that fire which is spread over [the surface] before the face. And things that are on the left appear on the right, because they touch opposite parts of the eyes with opposite parts. But right corresponds to right and left to left by a turning of the light, when these do not cohere with one another. This happens when the smoothness of mirrors has taken on height on this side and that, and so has thrust the right into the left part of the eyes and the left into the right. Faces are also seen upside down by the driving back of the light; and this, turning [them] round, renders lower the parts that are upper.

And all these things are of the kind that assist the causes of things; the god uses them as servants when he brings about the form of the best, so far as it can be done. But most people think that these are not assistants of causes but are themselves the causes of all things, since they have the power of cooling and heating, of solidifying and melting, yet they lack all intelligence and reason, which are found in no other nature except in soul. But soul escapes all perception of the eyes; whereas fire, air, water and earth are bodies, and they are seen.

But he who professes himself a lover of intelligence and wisdom must seek out first the causes belonging to the intelligent and wise nature, and then secondly those of the things which of necessity move others while they themselves are moved by others. Therefore I see that we must act thus: that we speak indeed of both kinds of causes, but separately of those which, with intelligence, are the producers of the most beautiful and best things, and of those which, lacking wisdom, produce things inconstant and disordered.

And of the causes of the eyes, so that they should have that power which they now have, I think enough has nearly been said. Next let their greatest usefulness, given to the human race by the gift of the gods, be set out. For the eyes have brought us the knowledge of the best things. For this discourse that we have held about the universe would never have been found, if neither the stars nor the sun nor the heaven could have come under the sight of the eyes. But now days and nights, known by the eyes, and then the revolutions of months and years, have devised number and measured out the span of time and driven [us] to the inquiry into the whole of nature; and from these things we have obtained philosophy, than which no good more desirable, none more excellent, either has been given to the race of mortals by the grant and gift of the gods or will be given * * *
